summary: Specifies a standard way to carry IP and ARP datagrams over ARCNET networks. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1201.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1051 specifies how IP and ARP data fit into ARCNET packets. It assigns a different identifying code to each kind of packet and describes how their addresses correspond.

questions: how to send ip over arcnet
what are the arcnet system codes
how are ip addresses mapped to arcnet
subtitle: How to carry IP and ARP packets inside ARCNET frames.

tldr.problem: IP datagrams and ARP packets need a defined way to travel over ARCNET networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC places each packet in an ARCNET frame and uses system code 240 for IP or 241 for ARP. It also describes packet-size handling and mapping Internet addresses to ARCNET node IDs.
tldr.outcome: This standard is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1201.

today: RFC 1051 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1201, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Carrying IP and ARP
sections.content: RFC 1051 defines a method for encapsulating Internet Protocol (IP) and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) datagrams on ARCNET. Each is transmitted in a standard ARCNET packet. The first data octet identifies the network-layer protocol: decimal 240 (hexadecimal F0) means IP, and 241 (F1) means ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: ARCNET carries the IP or ARP packet as data inside its own packet. The first data byte tells the receiver which kind it is.

sections.title: ARCNET Packet Sizes
sections.content: ARCNET supports normal packet data lengths of 1 to 253 octets and extended lengths of 257 to 508 octets, counting the system code. Lengths from 254 to 256 are forbidden. An IP packet in that range is padded with zero octets to reach 257; that padding is not counted in the IP header's total length. Where some hosts lack extended packet support, the IP MTU should be 253.
sections.plainLanguage: ARCNET has a gap in its allowed packet sizes. An IP packet that falls in the gap gets zero padding so the ARCNET packet reaches the minimum extended size.

sections.title: Mapping Network Addresses
sections.content: The RFC describes two recommended ways to map 32-bit Internet addresses to 8-bit ARCNET node IDs. One method uses the last eight bits of the Internet host number. Another uses ARP to discover mappings dynamically; ARP is optional. Implementations that support ARP must also be able to disable it and use host-number extraction. The broadcast Internet address maps to ARCNET node ID 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses and ARCNET node IDs have different lengths. A system can use the last eight host-number bits or look up a mapping with ARP.
